lesson_1.title: Your First Program
task: Welcome to the AlgoBlocks workspace! Let's write your first program. This task will show you how to make a function that simply gives back some text.
1. Open the 'Functions' tab and drag out a function block that has a 'return' slot. Name it 'hello'.
2. Open the 'Text' tab, retrieve a text block (the one with quotes), and type 'Hello World'.
3. Attach the text block to the function's return slot.
4. Look at the Python Code tab to see how your blocks turn into real code!

lesson_1.title: Returning Text
task: Working with text is a core part of programming. Let's practice making a function that gives back a specific word or symbol.
1. Open the 'Functions' tab, make a new return function, and name it 'draw_star'.
2. Grab a text block from the 'Text' tab and type '***'.
3. Attach the text block to the return slot.
4. Check the Python Code tab to see your code update automatically.

lesson_1.title: Using Inputs (Parameters)
task: Functions become powerful when we give them inputs (called parameters) to work with. Let's make a simple calculator!
1. Create a function named 'add'. Click the gear icon on the function block to add two inputs: name them 'a' and 'b'.
2. Open the 'Math' tab and drag out an addition block (+).
3. Open the 'Variables' tab, grab the 'a' and 'b' blocks, and snap them into the math block.
4. Attach the math block to the return slot.

lesson_1.title: Joining Text Together
task: You can combine text together to make friendly messages. This is called 'concatenation'.
1. Create a function named 'greet' with one input called 'name'.
2. Open the 'Text' tab and find the 'create text with' block.
3. Put a regular text block with 'Hi ' in the first slot, and the 'name' variable block in the second slot.

lesson_1.title: Making a List
task: A List (or Array) is a way to store multiple items in one place, like a shopping list.
2. Open the 'Lists (Built-in Type)' tab and grab a 'create list with' block.
3. Add three number blocks (1, 2, and 3) from the 'Math' tab into the list slots.

lesson_2.title: Storing Data in Variables
task: Variables are like labeled boxes where we can save information to use later.
2. Open the 'Variables' tab and click 'Create variable...'. Name it 'x'.
3. Drag out the 'set x to' block and attach the number 100 to it.
4. Now, grab the 'x' block from the 'Variables' tab and put it in the return slot.

lesson_2.title: Making Decisions (If/Else)
task: Programs can make choices based on rules you set. We use 'If/Else' blocks for this.
1. Make a function named 'is_positive' with an input 'n'.
2. Open the 'Logic' tab and get an 'if / do' block. Click the gear icon on the block to add an 'else' section.
3. Get a comparison block from the 'Logic' tab, and check if 'n > 0'.
4. If it's true (the 'do' part), return 'Yes'. In the 'else' part, return 'No'.

lesson_2.title: Repeating Actions (Loops)
task: Loops let us repeat instructions without writing the same code over and over.
3. Open the 'Loops' tab and get a 'repeat 5 times' block.
4. Inside the loop, go to the 'Math' tab and use the 'item += 1' block to change 'total' by 1.
5. After the loop finishes, return the 'total' variable.

lesson_2.title: Getting Items from a List
task: Every item in a list has a position number, called an 'index'. In programming, we start counting at 0, so the first item is at index 0.
1. Create a function 'get_first' with input 'arr' (short for array/list).
2. Open the 'Lists (Built-in Type)' tab and find the 'in list get' block.
3. Tell it to get the item at index 0 from the 'arr' list.

lesson_2.title: Adding to a List
task: We can add new items to lists we already made. This is called 'appending'.
2. Open the 'Lists (Built-in Type)' tab and find the 'append' block.

lesson_3.title: Checking How Fast Code Runs
task: The Complexity tab tells you how fast your code is! If your code takes the exact same number of steps no matter what, it gets a score of O(1), meaning 'Constant Time'.
3. Look at the Complexity tab. It is O(1) because doing one math problem is always fast, even if 'n' is a million!

lesson_3.title: Loops Make Code Take Longer
task: If you use a loop that repeats 'n' times, the code gets slower as 'n' gets bigger. The analyzer scores this as O(n), meaning 'Linear Time'.
3. Make a loop that repeats 'n' times.
5. Return 'total'. Check the Complexity tab to see the O(n) score!

lesson_3.title: Loops Inside Loops
task: Putting a loop inside another loop multiplies the work! If the outside repeats 'n' times and the inside repeats 'n' times, it gets a slower O(n²) score.
1. Create a function 'double_loop' with input 'n'. Set 'total' to 0.
2. Make an outer loop repeating 'n' times.
3. Put a second loop *inside* the first one, also repeating 'n' times.
4. Add 1 to 'total' inside the deepest loop.
5. Return 'total'. Look at how the Complexity tab meter rises to O(n²).

lesson_3.title: Checking Both Paths
task: When your code has an If/Else block, the analyzer looks at both paths to see which one takes the most work.
2. Make an If/Else block from the 'Logic' tab. Check if 'n > 10'.
3. Return 100 if true, and 0 if false.
4. Since returning a number is fast on both sides, the score stays a fast O(1).

lesson_3.title: Math is Faster than Loops
task: Sometimes you can use a math trick instead of a loop to make code run instantly! This turns a slow O(n) task into a fast O(1) task.
2. Use blocks from the 'Math' tab to build: n * (n + 1) / 2
3. Return the result. The analyzer sees no loops, so it scores a perfect O(1) Time!

lesson_4.title: Memory Usage
task: Your computer has to remember variables. The Space Complexity meter shows how much memory you are using.
4. Notice the Space meter says O(1). Creating one variable takes very little memory.

lesson_4.title: Fixed Memory Sizes
task: If you create a list that always has the exact same number of items, it also gets a fast O(1) Space score because the memory size never changes.
2. Make a new list from the 'Lists (Built-in Type)' tab with exactly two words: 'Apple' and 'Banana'.
3. Return the list. Check the Space score!

lesson_4.title: Growing Lists Use More Memory
task: If you add more items to a list based on an input 'n', the list gets bigger and uses more memory. This gets a Space score of O(n).
1. Create 'grow_list' with input 'n'. Start an empty list variable.
3. Inside the loop, use the 'append' block to add the number 1 to the list.
4. Return the list. Check the Space score!

lesson_4.title: Growing Text Uses Memory Too
task: Just like a list, if you keep adding letters to a piece of text inside a loop, the computer needs more memory to store the longer word.
1. Create 'build_text' with input 'n'. Set a variable to empty text ("").
3. Inside the loop, join the letter 'A' to your text variable.
4. Return the final text. Notice it also takes O(n) space!

lesson_4.title: Swapping Variables Cleanly
task: A good way to save memory is to swap variables directly instead of making temporary copies. Our workspace has a special 'swap' block for this!
1. Create a function 'swap_test' with inputs 'a' and 'b'.
2. Open the 'Variables' tab and drag out the 'swap variable' block. Set it to swap 'a' and 'b'.
3. Create a return list using the 'Lists (Built-in Type)' tab.
4. Put 'a' in the first slot and 'b' in the second slot.
